# CSV and XLSX Ingestion and Profiling

Auto-Mate reads a CSV or Excel workbook you attach to a task and shows what it understood about it: column names, inferred types, statistics, and a few real rows. All of that is computed **on your own computer**. Attaching a file sends nothing anywhere. No part of this feature calls a network service, an AI provider, or Python.

What this feature builds is a small, bounded description of each file called the **disclosure payload**. It is the only representation of your data the application is ever permitted to send anywhere. In this release nothing sends it: a later feature (disclosure review, FEAT-105) will show it to you and ask before anything is transmitted.

## What It Does

- The **New task** composer accepts up to five `.csv`, `.tsv`, or `.xlsx` files by drag-and-drop or through the file picker. Each file uploads with a progress bar, is analyzed, and then shows a preview panel.
- The preview lists every table (one for a CSV, one per worksheet), its row and column counts, each column's inferred type and statistics, the first 10 data rows, and plain-English findings such as "dates in `order_date` could be day/month or month/day".
- Starting the task attaches the analyzed files to it in the same database transaction that creates the task. A task never starts with half of its files attached.
- The original file is kept byte-for-byte for the life of the task and deleted with the task.

## How to Use It

Start the application with `pnpm dev`, open `http://127.0.0.1:5173/`, and in **New task**:

1. Describe the task.
2. Drop files onto **Attach CSV or Excel files (optional)**, or select the field and choose them. Keyboard users can reach the file field with Tab and open it with Enter or Space.
3. Wait for each file to show **Ready**. The **Start task** button stays disabled while any file is still uploading or being analyzed.
4. Review the preview. Use **Hide details** to collapse it, **Remove** to drop a file, or **Retry** after a failed upload.
5. Select **Start task**.

The browser checks each file's extension and size before uploading, using exactly the messages the server would return, so the two never disagree. The server's check is the one that counts.

The same flow is available through the local API:

```sh
curl -F file=@sales-q3.csv http://127.0.0.1:4317/api/uploads
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4317/api/tasks \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt":"Total the amount column by city","uploadIds":[1]}'
```

## What Leaves Your Machine, and What Never Does

Nothing leaves your machine in this release. The disclosure payload is prepared so that later features can show it to you and, with your approval, send it. It contains **exactly** this, and nothing else:

| Included                                                                                                           | Bound                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| File name (the last part only, never a folder), format, size in bytes, SHA-256 digest, detected text encoding       | Name cut to 200 characters                                         |
| Per table: sheet name, hidden flag, row and column counts, whether the row count is exact, header flag, delimiter   | —                                                                  |
| Per column: name, original name if it was renamed, inferred type and confidence, empty-cell counts, distinct count  | Names cut to 200 characters                                        |
| Per column: statistics (numeric range, mean, median, quartiles; date range and format; text length range)          | —                                                                  |
| Per column: up to 5 most frequent values                                                                           | **Only** when the column has fewer than 1,000 distinct values      |
| The first 10 data rows after the header                                                                             | Each cell cut to 200 characters, marked with `…`                   |
| Findings (the notes below) and a list of anything the size limit forced out                                        | At most 50 notes per table                                         |

The whole payload is capped at **64 KiB** of serialized text. It **never** contains:

- the rest of your file beyond those 10 sample rows;
- any frequent value from a column with 1,000 or more distinct values, or from a column holding a value longer than 200 characters (free text). Such a column reports "many" and no values at all, because the values are discarded while the file is read, not hidden afterwards;
- a folder path, from your computer or from the application's data directory.

When a description is larger than 64 KiB, it is reduced in a fixed order, and each step is recorded in the payload's `truncations` list so you can be told exactly what was left out:

1. `limit_notes`: more than 50 findings in one table are cut to 50 (always applied).
2. `drop_top_values`: frequent values are removed, largest table first.
3. `reduce_sample_rows`: sample rows are reduced from 10 toward 3 in every table.
4. `drop_sample_rows`: sample rows are removed from every table but the first.
5. `truncate_columns`: only the first columns of each table are kept, and the number left out is recorded.
6. `omit_tables`: trailing tables are dropped, as a last resort that makes the ceiling unconditional.

The same file always produces the same payload, byte for byte. Sampling for medians is seeded from the file's SHA-256, and no clock or randomness is involved. That is what makes approving a payload meaningful: what you approve is what would be sent.

These rules are enforced in four independent places: while the file is read (value tracking stops at the cardinality cap), when the profile is saved (the database refuses a high-cardinality column that carries values), when the payload is built (the 64 KiB ceiling), and by the payload's schema (it rejects an over-long sample cell or more than 10 sample rows).

## Supported File Shapes

The format is decided from the file's **content**, not its extension. A workbook saved with a `.csv` name is read as a workbook.

| File                                                            | Result                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Comma, semicolon, tab, or pipe separated text (`.csv`, `.tsv`)  | Read. The delimiter is detected.                                                                        |
| UTF-8 (with or without a byte-order mark), UTF-16 with a byte-order mark | Read.                                                                                           |
| Windows-1252 or Latin-1 text (a common Excel export)            | Read, with an "encoding guessed" finding.                                                               |
| Quoted fields containing delimiters, line breaks, or doubled quotes | Read as single values.                                                                              |
| Rows with more or fewer values than the rest, blank rows, footer rows | Read. They are counted and reported, not dropped silently.                                        |
| `.xlsx` workbooks, including hidden sheets, formulas, and merged cells | Every sheet is profiled, up to the sheet limit. Formulas contribute their last saved result.     |
| A workbook with a report title above the real header            | The title and blank rows are skipped and reported.                                                      |
| Legacy `.xls` (Excel 97–2003)                                   | Refused: "Open it in Excel and use Save As to save it as an Excel Workbook (.xlsx), then attach that file." |
| Word documents, archives, images, PDFs, executables             | Refused as not a CSV or Excel workbook.                                                                 |
| An empty file                                                   | Refused as empty.                                                                                       |

## How a File Is Read

1. **Format.** The first 64 KiB are inspected. A ZIP containing spreadsheet parts is `xlsx`. The legacy OLE2 signature is `.xls` and is refused. Text is `csv`. Anything else is refused.
2. **Encoding.** A byte-order mark decides it. Otherwise the file is checked as strict UTF-8, over the **whole file** when it is larger than the first 64 KiB, so an accented name on row 40,000 is still decoded correctly. If it is not valid UTF-8, it is read as Windows-1252.
3. **Dialect.** Comma, semicolon, tab, and pipe are each tried on the first records. The delimiter giving the most consistent number of fields per line wins, ties going to that order. A file where no delimiter splits lines is one column. The quote character and line ending are detected too, and each choice records a confidence.
4. **Header.** In a CSV, the first non-blank row is a header when every cell is non-empty text, no two cells repeat, and at least one column beneath it is a number, date, or true/false. A file with only one row keeps it as the header. In a workbook, the first 10 rows are scanned for a text row spanning at least two columns and half the table's width, followed by a row with a typed value. Header decisions are cosmetic, so they are made automatically and reported with a confidence.

Workbooks are read with a streaming reader. Memory stays flat as rows grow: a 300,001-row workbook profiles with bounded memory, and a test protects that.

## What Is Computed

For every column, in one pass over the rows and with memory that does not grow with the number of rows:

- **Counts**: missing cells, blank cells, and populated cells.
- **Type**: `integer`, `decimal`, `boolean`, `date`, `datetime`, `string`, or `empty`. A column gets a narrower type than text only when at least 99% of its values fit it. `typeConfidence` is the share that fit, and a column where some values do not fit is flagged mixed. Values like `0012` stay text, because a leading zero is meaningful in a zip code or account number. Numbers longer than 15 digits also stay text.
- **Dates**: `YYYY-MM-DD`, `YYYY/MM/DD`, `DD/MM/YYYY`, `MM/DD/YYYY`, `DD-MM-YYYY`, and `MM-DD-YYYY`, each optionally with a time, plus real date cells in workbooks. When day/month and month/day explain exactly the same values, which happens whenever every day is 12 or less, the column is marked **ambiguous** and both formats are recorded. The application does not guess. A column mixing two formats is text.
- **Statistics**: numeric minimum, maximum, mean, sample standard deviation, median, and quartiles. Percentiles are exact up to 10,000 numeric values and estimated above that. The output marks which. Date columns get a minimum, maximum, and format. Text columns get minimum, maximum, and mean length.
- **Frequent values**: the 5 most common values, only while a column has fewer than 1,000 distinct values.

## Findings

Anything that would change the meaning of your data is recorded as a finding rather than decided silently. Later features turn these into questions.

| Code                         | Meaning                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ambiguous_date_format`      | A date column reads equally well as day/month and month/day. Both formats are listed.                       |
| `mixed_type_column`          | Some values in a column do not fit its type. The count is given.                                            |
| `duplicate_headers_renamed`  | A repeated column name was renamed (`amount_2`). The original name is kept.                                 |
| `no_header_detected`         | No header row was found. Columns are named `column_1`, `column_2`, and so on.                               |
| `row_cap_reached`            | The row scan limit was reached. The row count is a lower bound.                                             |
| `leading_blank_rows_skipped` | Title or blank rows above the table were skipped.                                                           |
| `ragged_rows`                | Rows had a different number of values than the rest, often a total or footer row.                           |
| `blank_rows`                 | Blank rows were found and not counted as data.                                                              |
| `encoding_guessed`           | The encoding was inferred rather than certain.                                                              |
| `hidden_sheet`               | The worksheet is hidden in the workbook.                                                                    |
| `empty_sheet`                | The worksheet has no table.                                                                                 |
| `sheet_cap_reached`          | The workbook has more sheets than the limit. Only the first ones were read.                                 |
| `merged_cells`               | The sheet has merged cells, a sign it is a formatted report.                                                |
| `formula_cells`              | The sheet has formulas. Their last saved results were used.                                                 |

## Limits

Every limit is an environment variable. All values are **provisional**: the decision that will settle them (D14) is still open. When a limit is hit, the error names both the limit and the actual value.

| Variable                           | Default          | What it limits                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AUTOMATE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`        | `52428800` (50 MB) | Size of one file. Enforced while the file streams in, so an oversized upload is refused at once, not after it arrives. |
| `AUTOMATE_MAX_FILES_PER_TASK`      | `5`              | Files per task. May be lowered. It cannot be raised above 5, the ceiling in the request schema shared with the browser. |
| `AUTOMATE_MAX_PROFILE_ROWS`        | `1000000`        | Rows scanned per table. Beyond it the count is shown as "1,000,000+ rows (scan limit reached)".                  |
| `AUTOMATE_MAX_COLUMNS`             | `512`            | Columns per table.                                                                                               |
| `AUTOMATE_PARSE_TIMEOUT_MS`        | `60000`          | Time to read and profile one file. When it fires, the file stream is destroyed.                                  |
| `AUTOMATE_MAX_SHEETS`              | `20`             | Worksheets profiled per workbook.                                                                                |
| `AUTOMATE_MAX_INFLATED_BYTES`      | `1073741824` (1 GB) | How far a workbook may expand when unzipped. A quarter of it is the budget for the workbook's shared text table. |
| `AUTOMATE_STAGED_UPLOAD_TTL_HOURS` | `24`             | How long an upload may wait unattached before it is cleaned up.                                                  |

The sample-row count (10), cell length (200), payload ceiling (64 KiB), cardinality cap (1,000), frequent-value count (5), and median sample (10,000) are privacy policy (D04), not tuning knobs, so they are not environment variables.

## Storage and Retention

```text
~/.automate/                 (or AUTOMATE_HOME)
└── uploads/
    ├── staged/<uploadId>/<uploadId>-<name>   — before a task claims it
    └── <taskId>/<uploadId>-<name>            — for the life of the task
```

- Files are stored as uploaded, byte for byte, with their size and SHA-256 recorded. No converted copy is written.
- The stored name is derived from yours: folders, control characters, and leading dots are removed, accents are folded, other characters become `-`, and the name is cut to 100 characters. The upload id prefix keeps two files named `data.csv` from colliding. Your original name is kept only as a display label and is never used to build a path.
- Attaching a file to a task moves it from `staged/` into the task's folder. The move is a rename on the same disk, so it is atomic.
- **Retention (D12): life of the task.** An attached file is deleted with its task (the database cascade, plus a file sweep for the folder) and never on its own. Nothing is deleted because of its age.
- **Orphan cleanup.** At startup and every hour, uploads never attached to a task are removed once they are older than `AUTOMATE_STAGED_UPLOAD_TTL_HOURS`. So are staged folders with no database row, partial uploads older than an hour, and upload folders whose task no longer exists. This is housekeeping, not the retention policy.
- A file that fails analysis is kept, marked failed with its reason, so it can be retried or inspected. It is cleaned up like any other unattached upload.

## API

| Method and path                  | Purpose                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `POST /api/uploads`              | Multipart upload of exactly one file. Analyzes it and returns **201** with the upload, its table profiles, and its disclosure payload. |
| `GET /api/uploads/:id`           | One upload with its profiles and payload.                                                                                            |
| `DELETE /api/uploads/:id`        | Removes an unattached upload and its file. An attached upload is refused, because deleting its task is how it is deleted.            |
| `GET /api/tasks/:taskId/uploads` | A task's uploads. Not paginated, deliberately: a task holds at most five files.                                                      |
| `POST /api/tasks`                | Accepts an optional `uploadIds` array (at most 5, no repeats). Each must exist, be unattached, and be analyzed, or no task is created. |

State-changing routes apply the same `Origin`/`Host` check as the rest of the API. Responses carry only `filePath`, relative to the data root. No response field holds an absolute path.

| Code                      | Status | When                                                                                   |
| ------------------------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `UPLOAD_NOT_FOUND`        | 404    | The upload id does not exist.                                                          |
| `UPLOAD_ALREADY_ATTACHED` | 409    | The upload belongs to a task already.                                                  |
| `UPLOAD_TOO_LARGE`        | 413    | The file passed `AUTOMATE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`.                                           |
| `UNSUPPORTED_FILE_FORMAT` | 415    | The content is not delimited text or an `.xlsx` workbook (including legacy `.xls`).   |
| `UPLOAD_LIMIT_REACHED`    | 400    | A task would hold more files than `AUTOMATE_MAX_FILES_PER_TASK`.                       |
| `FILE_EMPTY`              | 400    | The file has no content.                                                               |
| `PARSE_FAILED`            | 422    | The file could not be read. The message names the line or sheet.                       |
| `PARSE_TIMEOUT`           | 422    | Reading took longer than `AUTOMATE_PARSE_TIMEOUT_MS`.                                  |
| `TOO_MANY_COLUMNS`        | 422    | A table is wider than `AUTOMATE_MAX_COLUMNS`.                                          |
| `WORKBOOK_TOO_LARGE`      | 422    | A workbook expanded past `AUTOMATE_MAX_INFLATED_BYTES` or its shared-text budget.     |
| `NO_TABULAR_CONTENT`      | 422    | No rows with values were found.                                                        |

A request with no file part, more than one file part, or a transfer interrupted midway returns `VALIDATION_ERROR`. After a 422 the upload row stays, marked failed, and its file is kept.

## Logging

The server logs upload and profile ids, byte sizes, formats, table/row/column counts, durations, detected delimiter and encoding, and column **types**. It never logs a file name, a cell value, a sample row, a frequent value, or a statistic. Those are the data the disclosure bound exists to protect.

## Security Posture

This developer preview runs generated code without an enforced isolation boundary, and nothing in this feature changes that. The upload limit, the storage layout, the decompression budget, and the parse timeout are availability guards for a local preview. They are not a sandbox, and they do not keep generated code away from your files.

What this feature does guarantee is narrow:

- nothing is transmitted;
- the disclosure payload is bounded as described above;
- high-cardinality values are never kept;
- upload paths cannot escape the data directory;
- file content never reaches a log;
- file content is shown in the browser as text only: never as HTML, never as a link. Cells starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` are shown literally and marked, not treated as formulas.

## Dependency Record

Recorded so the next person does not redo this investigation.

- **Node, not Python.** Profiling is TypeScript in the server. The Python runtime belongs to a later feature, and startup treats a missing `uv` or Python as a warning. So the first thing a new developer tries, attaching a file, must work without Python.
- **`exceljs` 4.4.0, streaming reader only.** Measured on a 300,001-row, 11.4 MB workbook with Node 24.15: the streaming `WorkbookReader` took 4.2 s and retained 35 MB. Loading the whole workbook took 6.2 s, retained 732 MB, and ran out of memory under a 256 MB heap. `read-excel-file` took 3.0 s but retained 248 MB. Only streaming stays flat as files grow. The in-memory loader is never used, and a test fails if it appears outside fixture generation.
- **Two contained interventions in the unzip layer.** `exceljs` exposes no hook there, so the reader intercepts the input stream's `pipe` for two purposes:
  1. to count decompressed bytes per entry, for the inflation budget;
  2. to suppress a premature `end` event. `unzipper` 0.10.14 emits it while parsed entries are still buffered, and `exceljs` then silently drops them. That includes `xl/workbook.xml` when it comes last, as it does in workbooks written with ZIP data descriptors. Without the fix those files fail to open.
  Both rely on internals of the exactly pinned versions, and tests fail loudly if an upgrade changes them.
- **`uuid` override to 14.0.2.** `exceljs` pulls `uuid@8`, which is inside the advisory range `<11.1.1`. A pnpm override lifts the whole tree to zero advisories. `exceljs` uses only the named `v4` export, which uuid 14 still provides. If you re-pin, stay at or above `11.1.1`: `11.1.0` is still affected.
- **`csv-parse` 7.0.2** streams CSV and TSV, and **`busboy` 1.6.0** parses multipart uploads. Using `busboy` directly, rather than a wrapper, lets the size cap, hash, and probe run while the bytes stream to disk.
- **No encoding library.** Node's full-ICU `TextDecoder` handles every encoding needed, and its strict UTF-8 mode is the detector.
- **Rejected:**
  - `xlsx` (SheetJS) from npm is frozen at 0.18.5 with unfixed advisories; the fixes exist only in a CDN-published build.
  - `@e965/xlsx` is an unofficial republish of that project.
  - `read-excel-file` keeps the whole sheet in memory, about 22 times the file size.
  - `multer` and `formidable` are wrappers over `busboy` that add a temp-file hop.
  - `iconv-lite` and `chardet` are unnecessary.

## Known Limitations

- A CSV whose columns are all text (names, cities, emails) is read as having **no header**, with a `no_header_detected` finding. The header rule needs at least one typed column to tell a header row from data. A CSV whose header repeats a name is treated the same way. Workbooks rename repeated header names instead.
- Comma decimals (`3,50`) are read as text, not numbers.
- Worksheets are read in the order the file stores them. Each profile records its true position in the workbook.
- A workbook that stores its sheets before its shared text is spooled to temporary files while reading. Those files are removed afterwards, or when the server exits if reading stops early.
